name: Sephardi

database_scope.purpose: Sourced reference for Sephardi minhagim and halachic practice. It records what the cited sources say, with a confidence level for each entry, and is not a psak.
database_scope.coverage_note: 26 sourced topics and 5 distinctive customs, compiled from the cited sources in October 2026. Each entry carries a confidence level (well-attested, disputed, regional, needs-review). 19 topics have no community-specific source and are listed under 'gaps' rather than filled with generic text.

identity.primary_origin: The Iberian Peninsula (Spain and Portugal), before the expulsions of the 1490s
secondary_centers: Safed, where the Shulchan Aruch was composed in 1563
Western Sephardi centres: Amsterdam, London (Bevis Marks) and New York (Shearith Israel, founded 1654)
The Ottoman lands, Syria, Iraq and North Africa

languages: Judeo-Spanish: for example the 'Morir habemos' exchange on Tisha B'Av in Amsterdam and New York
Portuguese: honours are announced in Portuguese in London, where Ladino is not used

subgroups.name: Western Sephardi (Spanish and Portuguese)
subgroups.note: Amsterdam, London (Bevis Marks / Sha'ar Asamayim), New York (Shearith Israel, founded 1654) and daughter communities. Rite described by its own exponents as non-kabbalistic. Distinct pronunciation and Portuguese/Spanish liturgical usages.

subgroups.name: Eastern Sephardi / Mizrahi
subgroups.note: Communities of the former Ottoman lands, Syria (Aleppo/Damascus), Iraq (Baghdad), North Africa (Morocco etc.). Liturgy shaped by Lurianic kabbalah. Practice rests heavily on Shulchan Arukh, Ben Ish Chai and Kaf HaChaim. Regional variants recorded per entry.

subgroups.name: Jerusalemite Sephardi
subgroups.note: Old Yishuv Sephardi practice in Jerusalem; documented here only where a source explicitly names a Jerusalem custom (e.g., Kaf HaChaim on hagbaha; meat during all Nine Days).

subgroups.name: Modern Israeli Sephardi
subgroups.note: Contemporary practice shaped largely by R. Ovadia Yosef (Yabia Omer, Yechaveh Da'at, Chazon Ovadia) and Yalkut Yosef, plus R. Eliezer Melamed's Peninei Halakha which records Sephardi practice alongside Ashkenazi.

timeline.event: R. Yosef Karo composes the Shulchan Arukh (1563) on the basis of his Beit Yosef.
timeline.halachic_impact: Becomes the binding code ('Maran') for Sephardic and Eastern communities; the Rema's glosses mark where Ashkenazi custom differs.

timeline.event: R. Israel Najara (born Damascus c. 1555) publishes Zemirot Yisrael (Safed 1587; Salonica 1599/1600; Venice 1600).
timeline.halachic_impact: His piyyutim become a core layer of the bakashot repertoire in Aleppo and Morocco.

timeline.event: Twenty-three Jews of mostly Spanish-Portuguese origin from Recife, Brazil landed in New Amsterdam in September 1654 and founded Congregation Shearith Israel; they won permission from the Dutch West India Company to remain in 1655, and it was the only Jewish congregation in New York City from 1654 until 1825 (Shearith Israel, 'Congregational History'). Its earliest extant constitution dates from 1728 and is written in both English and Portuguese.
timeline.halachic_impact: Establishes the Spanish-Portuguese minhag in North America; services conducted according to that rite to this day.

timeline.event: Miqra Qodesh compiled by R. Mordechai Abadi in Aleppo (1872); Shir Yedidot printed in Marrakesh (1921).
timeline.halachic_impact: Fix the Aleppo (same order each week) and Moroccan (weekly-changing) bakashot traditions.

timeline.event: Mass immigration of Middle Eastern and North African Jews; R. Ovadia Yosef's rulings and Yalkut Yosef become widely followed.
timeline.halachic_impact: Partial standardization of Israeli Sephardi practice around Maran, alongside surviving regional customs (e.g., Moroccan rice abstention, Mimouna).

primary_codes: Beit Yosef (R. Yosef Karo) on the Tur
later_poskim: Ben Ish Chai (R. Yosef Hayyim of Baghdad)
R. Ovadia Yosef: Yabia Omer, Yechaveh Da'at, Chazon Ovadia
core_halachic_authorities.decision_principle: Eastern and modern Israeli Sephardim generally rule according to the Shulchan Arukh (Maran) where the Rema records a differing Ashkenazi custom, with local and kabbalistic (Lurianic) customs layered on top. The Western Spanish-Portuguese rite preserves an older, relatively non-kabbalistic order.

runtime.practice_baseline: Practice rests on the Shulchan Arukh and Beit Yosef of R. Yosef Karo, as applied by the Ben Ish Chai, Kaf HaChaim and, in modern Israel, R. Ovadia Yosef and Yalkut Yosef; the Western Spanish-Portuguese rite follows its own congregational tradition.

halacha_index.topic: Nusach and character of the rite
halacha_index.summary: Eastern and Israeli Sephardim pray in a Sephardi/Edot HaMizrach nusach shaped by Lurianic kabbalah; the Western Spanish-Portuguese rite is explicitly described by its exponents as non-kabbalistic.
common_practices: Service follows Shulchan Arukh rubrics
Much of the Western service is read aloud and sung by the congregation together with the Hazzan

variants.practice: Tradition described as 'a non-kabbalistic one'; relatively few kabbalistic additions. At Shearith Israel, 'much of the service is read aloud and sung by the congregation together with the Hazzan', and each holiday has its own melody.
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag (R. Jonathan Cohen), 'Kabbalah - not' page; Sephardic Studies, 'The Spanish and Portuguese Synagogue' (Shearith Israel)

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, sites.google.com/site/londonsephardiminhag/kabbalah-not; sephardicstudies.org/csi.html
halacha_index.review_notes: No Eastern siddur was opened for this entry; the Eastern nusach description is general and should be checked against a specific siddur (e.g., Tefillat Yesharim, Kol Ya'akov, Yalkut Yosef siddur).
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים מזרחיים וישראלים מתפללים בנוסח ספרדי/עדות המזרח שעוצב בידי הקבלה הלוריאנית; הנוסח הספרדי-פורטוגזי המערבי מתואר במפורש בידי נציגיו כבלתי קבלי.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim rise before dawn to say selichot and tachanunim from (the day after) Rosh Chodesh Elul until Yom Kippur.
common_practices: Selichot daily through Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance
Selichot are not said on Rosh Chodesh itself, because vidduy is not recited on Rosh Chodesh
halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 581:1 (Rema records that Ashkenazim begin only shortly before Rosh Hashana); Kaf HaChaim 581:15; Chazon Ovadia, Yamim Nora'im p. 2 (as cited by OU, 'Halacha According to the Sephardic Practice: The Month of Elul')
halacha_index.review_notes: Arukh HaShulchan OC 581 likewise records that 'the Sefardi communities have the custom to say these prayers from the beginning of Elul until after Yom Kippur.'
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים קמים לפני עלות השחר לומר סליחות ותחנונים מ(היום שאחרי) ראש חודש אלול ועד יום כיפור.

halacha_index.summary: Most Sephardic women recite the blessing 'lehadlik ner shel Shabbat' before lighting, following the general rule that a blessing precedes the mitzvah.
common_practices: Blessing first, then lighting

variants.practice: R. Ovadia Yosef rules that Sephardim recite the blessing before kindling.
variants.source: Yechaveh Da'at 2:33 (as cited in Torah.org, Weekly Halacha 5767 Shavuos, n. 15)

variants.subgroup: Families with an established practice of blessing after lighting; Western (Spanish-Portuguese)
variants.practice: Some poskim say those with a family practice of blessing after lighting may continue it; for the S&P rite, the London Sephardi Minhag states that 'the original S&P custom in both these cases is unclear, so it cannot be said that either option is incorrect.'
variants.source: Halachipedia, 'Shabbat Candles', section 'The order of candle lighting'; London Sephardi Minhag (R. Jonathan Cohen), 'Shabbat' page, Note 1

halacha_index.source: Yechaveh Da'at 2:33; Shulchan Arukh OC 263:5 (as cited in secondary sources)
halacha_index.review_notes: Shulchan Arukh OC 263:5 was not opened directly. Do not present blessing-after as 'wrong' for Sephardic families with that tradition.
halacha_index.summary_he: רוב הנשים הספרדיות מברכות "להדליק נר של שבת" לפני ההדלקה, לפי הכלל שברכה קודמת למצווה.

halacha_index.summary: In the Western Spanish-Portuguese rite, the Friday-evening service traditionally opens with Psalm 29 (Mizmor leDavid) and Psalm 92, without the six-psalm sequence 95-99.

variants.practice: Psalm 29 and Psalm 92 form the preliminary Kabbalat Shabbat; melodies documented in London and Bayonne. Text attested in Isaac Pinto's 1765-66 New York prayer book.
variants.source: Milken Archive of Jewish Music, 'Shabbat' (Jewish Voices in the New World), liner notes by Neil W. Levin

variants.practice: Many Eastern communities recite Shir HaShirim between Minha and Kabbalat Shabbat (not the Spanish-Portuguese custom).
variants.source: Wikipedia, 'Sephardic law and customs'

halacha_index.source: Milken Archive of Jewish Music, 'Shabbat', Western Sephardi tradition
halacha_index.review_notes: Eastern Kabbalat Shabbat order (whether Psalms 95-99 precede Psalm 29) was not verified in an Eastern siddur; Shir HaShirim custom rests on a Wikipedia lead only and needs a primary source.
halacha_index.summary_he: בנוסח הספרדי-פורטוגזי המערבי נפתחת תפילת ערב שבת במסורת במזמור כט (מזמור לדוד) ובמזמור צב, בלי רצף ששת המזמורים צה-צט.

halacha_index.summary: In London Spanish-Portuguese usage, Shalom Aleichem and Eshet Hayil are not part of the traditional custom, and the priestly blessing was traditionally given only on festivals.

variants.practice: According to the London Sephardi Minhag, 'some ten or fifteen years ago' (no year given) the London kahal voted to part with the 350-year-old tradition and introduce Birkat Cohanim on Shabbat; 'no other S&P communities have followed suit', while among North African and Eastern Sephardim it is performed every Shabbat.
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag (R. Jonathan Cohen), 'Shabbat' page

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Shabbat' page
halacha_index.review_notes: Single personal (though expert) source; verify against the Bevis Marks or Shearith Israel minhag.
halacha_index.summary_he: במנהג הספרדי-פורטוגזי בלונדון "שלום עליכם" ו"אשת חיל" אינם חלק מהמנהג המסורתי, וברכת כהנים ניתנה במסורת רק בחגים.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim hold a structured 'seder' of symbolic foods on the night(s) of Rosh Hashana, saying a Yehi Ratzon over each.
common_practices: Foods listed by Shulchan Arukh: beans (rubia/lubia), leeks, beets (silka), dates, pumpkin/gourd; commonly also pomegranate, apple in honey, and a head (of a ram or fish)
Ben Ish Chai's order begins with the date (ha'etz said over it, as one of the Seven Species), then lubia, leek, chard, gourd, pomegranate, apple
Yehi Ratzon recited after taking a bite, to avoid an interruption between blessing and eating
If a food cannot be eaten, one may look at it and say the Yehi Ratzon (Kaf HaChaim)
Most do the simanim on both nights; some only on the first

variants.practice: Order and wording follow Ben Ish Chai; head of a male (rooster) preferred.
variants.source: Ben Ish Chai, Year One, Nitzavim 4; Kaf HaChaim 583:7, 583:11, 583:25

variants.practice: Sugar and sesame seeds may replace fenugreek/string beans.
variants.source: My Jewish Learning, 'How To Lead A Sephardic Rosh Hashanah Seder' (citing Rahel Musleah)

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 583:1; Ben Ish Chai, Nitzavim 4; Kaf HaChaim 583
halacha_index.review_notes: The order of foods is not halachically critical; differing family orders are legitimate.
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים עורכים "סדר" מובנה של מאכלי סמל בליל (או בלילות) ראש השנה, ואומרים "יהי רצון" על כל אחד.

halacha_index.summary: The Shulchan Arukh rules that the kaparot custom should be stopped, following the Rashba and Ramban; nonetheless many Sephardic communities adopted it under kabbalistic influence.

variants.practice: Do not perform kaparot; some recommend money instead of chickens.
variants.source: Shulchan Arukh OC 605:1; R. Haim David Halevy, Mekor Hayyim 4:216 (as cited by jewishideas.org)

variants.practice: Perform kaparot (often with chickens), following later kabbalistic sources (Ari, cited by Magen Avraham 605:1).
variants.source: Chabad.org, 'Shulchan Aruch: Chapter 605' notes: 'His view... is upheld today by many Sephardim, though others have adopted this custom.'

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 605:1
halacha_index.review_notes: Do not tell a Sephardic user that kaparot is either required or forbidden for them; family custom varies.
halacha_index.summary_he: השולחן ערוך פוסק שיש לבטל את מנהג הכפרות, בהתאם לרשב"א ולרמב"ן; אף על פי כן אימצו אותו קהילות ספרדיות רבות בהשפעה קבלית.

halacha_index.summary: At Shearith Israel, those listed in the Book of Perpetual Hashcabot are memorialized on Yom Kippur and at other fixed times.

variants.practice: A hashcaba for those listed is recited before services on Rosh Hodesh mornings and on the Shabbat afternoon after each person's anniversary of death, and they are also memorialized on Yom Kippur; the book dates back to 1718 and includes the names of congregants who left bequests for the future maintenance of the synagogue.
variants.source: Congregation Shearith Israel, 'Life Cycle Events' page

halacha_index.source: Congregation Shearith Israel, Life Cycle Events
halacha_index.review_notes: Wording checked on the full Shearith Israel 'Life Cycle Events' page.
halacha_index.summary_he: בבית הכנסת שערית ישראל מזכירים את הרשומים בספר ההשכבות התמידיות ביום כיפור ובמועדים קבועים אחרים.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim do not wear tefillin on Chol HaMoed.
common_practices: No tefillin on Chol HaMoed of Pesach or Sukkot
halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh OC 31:2; Beit Yosef OC 31 (the Spanish communities originally wore them per the Rosh, but stopped on seeing the Zohar); Kaf HaChaim 31:6 (as cited by shulchanaruchharav.com, 'Tefillin on Chol Hamoed')
halacha_index.review_notes: No Spanish-Portuguese-specific statement was found on this; the general Sephardic rule is applied to them only by inference, so the app should not assert it for S&P without review.
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים אינם מניחים תפילין בחול המועד.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim wind the arm strap outward over the arm and back in under it.

variants.practice: 'Like all Sephardim the S&P wind the strap outwards over the arm, and back in under it.'
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Tephillin' page

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Tephillin' page
halacha_index.review_notes: Single source; the claim that this applies to 'all Sephardim' was not independently verified.
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים כורכים את רצועת היד כלפי חוץ מעל הזרוע וחזרה פנימה מתחתיה.

halacha_index.topic: Tallit and tefillin on Tisha B'Av
halacha_index.summary: Practice differs: some Sephardic communities wear neither tallit nor tefillin until Minha, while others wear tefillin in the morning.

variants.practice: 'Tallet and Tefillin are worn only at Minha.'
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Fast of Ab' page

variants.practice: No tallit or tefillin at Shacharit; the hazzan and those at the Torah also do not wear a tallit.
variants.source: Halachipedia, 'When to Wear Tefillin', Tisha Be'Av section

variants.practice: Wear tefillin at Shacharit until kinot, or at home before coming to synagogue.
variants.source: Halachipedia, 'When to Wear Tefillin', Tisha Be'Av section

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, Fast of Ab; Halachipedia, When to Wear Tefillin
halacha_index.review_notes: Ask the user's specific community; no single Sephardic rule.
halacha_index.summary_he: המנהגים שונים: קהילות ספרדיות אחדות אינן עוטות טלית ותפילין עד המנחה, ואחרות מניחות תפילין בבוקר.

halacha_index.summary: The Western rite has distinctive Tisha B'Av customs.

variants.practice: People called to the Torah at Shacharit are called only as 'Cohen', 'Levi', 'Shelishi' without their names; a deliberately makeshift black curtain hangs before the Hechal doors; the Haftara is read verse by verse interspersed with a Spanish commentary.
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Fast of Ab' page

variants.practice: Greeting 'Morir habemos' answered 'Ya lo sabemos'; described as unknown in London.
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Fast of Ab' page

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Fast of Ab' page
halacha_index.review_notes: Single expert source; regional to S&P congregations.
halacha_index.summary_he: לנוסח המערבי מנהגים מיוחדים בתשעה באב.

halacha_index.summary: Most Sephardim eat meat and drink wine on Rosh Chodesh Av, abstaining from the end of that day, and continue abstaining until the end of the 10th of Av.
common_practices: Meat permitted on Rosh Chodesh Av
Abstention from the 2nd of Av
Stringent until the end of the day on the 10th of Av

variants.practice: R. Ovadia Yosef cites the Jerusalem custom of abstaining from meat during all Nine Days.
variants.source: R. David Pardo, 'Hilkhot Shiva Asar b'Tammuz v'Yemei Bein HaMeitzarim 5775' (OU-JLIC), n. 7

variants.practice: Abstain only during the week in which Tisha B'Av falls (one of three customs recorded in Shulchan Arukh).
variants.source: Shulchan Arukh OC 551:9

halacha_index.source: Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 8:13 ('Meat and Wine'), citing Mishnah Berurah 551:58 and Kaf HaChaim 551:125; Yechaveh Da'at 1:41 (as cited by Jewish Link)
halacha_index.review_notes: Variants are real; communities stricter than the majority (Jerusalem) should not be told meat on Rosh Chodesh is their custom.
halacha_index.summary_he: רוב הספרדים אוכלים בשר ושותים יין בראש חודש אב, ונמנעים מסוף אותו יום, וממשיכים להימנע עד סוף העשירי באב.

halacha_index.summary: Most Sephardim apply the laundering prohibition only in the week in which Tisha B'Av falls; when Tisha B'Av falls on Sunday there is no such week.
common_practices: Laundry restricted only in shavua shechal bo
If Tisha B'Av is on Sunday, the restriction applies only on Tisha B'Av itself
Haircuts avoided in the week before even according to Sephardim
halacha_index.source: Peninei Halakha (R. Eliezer Melamed), 'Customs of the Nine Days' (Arutz Sheva); Shulchan Arukh OC 551:3-4; shulchanaruchharav.com, 'Sefaradi versus Ashkenazi customs during the Three Weeks'
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Melamed notes the lenient custom 'was prevalent in Sephardic communities around the Land of Israel (Shulchan Gavoha 551:49) and in some communities in North Africa.'
halacha_index.summary_he: רוב הספרדים מחילים את איסור הכביסה רק בשבוע שבו חל תשעה באב; כשתשעה באב חל ביום ראשון אין שבוע כזה.

halacha_index.summary: Sources conflict on whether Sephardim hold weddings between 17 Tammuz and Rosh Chodesh Av.

variants.practice: Weddings permitted until Rosh Chodesh Av; prohibited from Rosh Chodesh until after Tisha B'Av.
variants.source: Shulchan Arukh and Rema OC 551:1-2 (as summarized by OU Torah, 'Marriage During the Three Weeks')

variants.practice: Sephardim generally avoid weddings during all Three Weeks as an inauspicious time.
variants.source: Wikipedia, 'The Nine Days'

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh OC 551:1-2
halacha_index.review_notes: Unresolved conflict; refer to community rabbi.
halacha_index.summary_he: המקורות סותרים אם ספרדים עורכים חתונות בין י"ז בתמוז לראש חודש אב.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardic mourning customs run from the start of the Omer until the morning of the 34th day; on Lag BaOmer itself music and dancing are permitted in honor of R. Shimon bar Yochai's hillula, but haircuts and weddings are not, and music resumes being prohibited on the night of the 34th.
common_practices: No haircuts or shaving until the morning of the 34th
Rosh Chodesh Iyar is included; cutting hair then is called 'a mistake' by Shulchan Arukh
Music and dancing allowed on Lag BaOmer for the hillula
All restrictions lapse shortly after daybreak of the 34th (part of a day counts as a whole day)

variants.practice: End all mourning customs on Lag BaOmer (the 33rd).
variants.source: R. Eliezer Melamed, 'Customs of Mourning during the Omer Period' (Revivim)

variants.practice: No haircuts until erev Shavuot.
variants.source: R. Eliezer Melamed, 'Customs of Mourning during the Omer Period' (Revivim)

variants.practice: Weddings already on Lag BaOmer.
variants.source: Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 3:4

variants.practice: R. Ovadia Yosef writes that women are not included in the haircut restriction, though it is fitting to be stringent where not needed.
variants.source: Chazon Ovadia, Sefirat HaOmer 36 (as quoted in a Sefaria source sheet)

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 493:1-3; Peninei Halakha, Zemanim 3:2 and 3:4; R. Eliezer Melamed, 'Customs of Mourning during the Omer Period'
halacha_index.review_notes: R. Melamed adds that although most Sephardim in Israel do not follow the Turkish/Egyptian leniency, in great need one may ask a Torah scholar.
halacha_index.summary_he: מנהגי האבלות הספרדיים נמשכים מתחילת העומר עד בוקר היום ה-34; בל"ג בעומר עצמו מותרים מוזיקה וריקודים לכבוד הילולת רבי שמעון בר יוחאי, אך לא תספורת וחתונות, והמוזיקה חוזרת להיאסר בליל ה-34.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim never accepted the kitniyot prohibition and eat rice and legumes on Pesach, checking them for stray grain; several regional communities abstain from rice.
common_practices: Kitniyot eaten
Rice must be bought in packages certified kosher for Pesach or checked thoroughly three times (Peninei Halakha, Pesach 9:2, citing Ama Devar 1:62)

variants.practice: Custom not to eat rice on Pesach.
variants.source: Lev Chayim 2:94 (as cited in Peninei Halakha, Pesach 9:2)

variants.practice: Many Moroccan Jews refrain from rice and other dry kitniyot on Pesach.
variants.source: Peninei Halakha, Pesach 9:2

variants.practice: Many laypeople did not eat rice; those who did checked it two or three times.
variants.source: Ben Ish Chai, Year One, Tzav 41 (as cited in Peninei Halakha, Pesach 9:2)

halacha_index.source: Beit Yosef OC 453 ('nobody worries about such things except for Ashkenazim'); Peninei Halakha, Pesach 9:2 'The Sephardic Custom'; Ama Devar 1:62
halacha_index.review_notes: Peninei Halakha: 'Each person should continue his ancestral custom.' Spices such as cumin, turmeric and fenugreek need inspection.
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים מעולם לא קיבלו את איסור הקטניות ואוכלים אורז וקטניות בפסח, ובודקים אותם לגרעינים תועים; כמה קהילות אזוריות נמנעות מאורז.

halacha_index.summary: Moroccan (and broader Maghrebi) Jews celebrate Mimouna on the night and day after Pesach with open homes and festive sweets.
common_practices: Open house with sweets such as mufleta
Blessings and visits between families
Muslim neighbors historically brought flour after Pesach

variants.practice: One of the earliest references, according to Aish.com, is the diary of an unnamed 18th-century Jewish traveler from Italy, who recorded that 'on the final night of Passover, Moroccan Jews set the table with different kinds of fish and greet and bless each other'; some went at dawn to water sources.
variants.source: Aish.com, 'Mimouna: The Ultimate Passover Afterparty'; Chabad.org, 'Unpacking the Secrets of Mimouna'

halacha_index.source: My Jewish Learning, 'Mimouna: A Post-Passover Celebration'; Chabad.org, 'Unpacking the Secrets of Mimouna'
halacha_index.review_notes: Origins are disputed (yahrzeit of R. Maimon, Arabic 'ma'amoun', 'ani ma'amin', folk/pagan roots). Not a halachic obligation; not a practice of Western S&P communities.

references.title: Mimouna, a Unique Moroccan Jewish Tradition

halacha_index.summary_he: יהודי מרוקו (והמגרב הרחב) חוגגים מימונה בלילה וביום שאחרי פסח, עם בתים פתוחים וממתקי חג.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim light one menorah per household, adding one light each night, kindled by the head of the household on behalf of all.
common_practices: One chanukiah per household
Lights increase from one to eight
halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 671:2 (Maran follows Tosafot; the Rema rules each household member lights); Kaf HaChaim 671:6; Yedei Chayim 671:3 (as cited by OU, 'Hilchot and Minhagei Chanukah According to the Sephardic Practice')
halacha_index.review_notes: The Taz notes this is a rare case where Sephardim follow Tosafot. Students away from home raise separate questions; refer to a rabbi.

references.title: Sephardic Chanukah Lighting in a Yeshiva or University Dormitory - The Jewish Link

halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים מדליקים חנוכייה אחת לכל בית, ומוסיפים נר בכל לילה, והיא מודלקת בידי בעל הבית בשם כולם.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim raise and display the open Torah scroll before the reading, not after.
common_practices: Scroll opened (traditionally three columns) and shown to all sides before reading
Congregation points at the text and says 'Vezot HaTorah'

variants.practice: Custom was to walk around the entire synagogue with the open scroll so all could see the text.
variants.source: Kaf HaChaim 134:13 (as cited in Sefaria sheet 'Hagba: Lifting the Torah, Uplifting Ourselves')

halacha_index.source: Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 134:2 (Rema: Ashkenazi custom after reading); Ben Ish Chai, Year Two, Toldot 16 (as cited by Jewish Action); Masechet Soferim 14:14
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים מגביהים ומציגים את ספר התורה הפתוח לפני הקריאה, ולא אחריה.

halacha_index.summary: The London Spanish-Portuguese tradition has a distinctive Hebrew pronunciation.

variants.practice: Ayin traditionally pronounced 'ng' (e.g., 'Ba-ngaboor', 'Be-ngalma'); no distinction between bet with and without dagesh (both 'b'); pure vowels (segol and tsere both as in 'let'); vocal vs silent sheva and milra/mil'el stress strictly observed; 'Kal' for kol (Kal Nidrey).
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Pronunciation' page

variants.practice: Moseh Abudiente's Grammatica hebraica describes ayin as 'Hgayn' with sound 'Hg'.
variants.source: Academic paper on Western Sephardic Hebrew pronunciation

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Pronunciation' page
halacha_index.review_notes: Source notes the 'ng' ayin is now often ignored but ayin is still not treated as aleph. Torah cantillation (te'amim) melodies for any subgroup were not documented.
halacha_index.summary_he: למסורת הספרדית-הפורטוגזית בלונדון הגיית עברית מיוחדת.

halacha_index.summary: In London, the announcement of who receives synagogue honours (mitsvot) has always been made in Portuguese; Ladino is not used there.

variants.practice: Portuguese for mitsvot announcements; older community terms such as 'Sa'ar Asamayim', 'Heshaim', 'Askamot', 'Echal'.
variants.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Pronunciation' page

halacha_index.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Pronunciation' page
halacha_index.summary_he: בלונדון ההכרזה על מי שמקבל כיבודים בבית הכנסת (מצוות) נעשית מאז ומתמיד בפורטוגזית; לדינו אינה משמשת שם.

halacha_index.summary: Beit Yosef warns against eating fish with milk for reasons of danger; many Sephardim avoid fish with dairy, but the scope of the custom differs.

variants.practice: R. Ovadia Yosef recommends refraining at least from fish with milk, even if some are lenient with fish and butter.
variants.source: Yechaveh Da'at 6:46 (as cited by Yeshivat Har Etzion VBM, 'More Precautionary Prohibitions')

variants.practice: Some Sephardim refrain even from cheese with fish (e.g., tuna melts); others are lenient.
variants.source: Yeshivat Har Etzion VBM, 'More Precautionary Prohibitions'

halacha_index.source: Beit Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 87; Taz YD 87:3 and Darkhei Moshe (who regard the Beit Yosef text as a scribal error for 'meat')
halacha_index.review_notes: The Shulchan Arukh YD 87:3 itself states fish and dairy are not prohibited even rabbinically as basar bechalav; the concern is only the Beit Yosef's health warning.
halacha_index.summary_he: הבית יוסף מזהיר מאכילת דג עם חלב משום סכנה; ספרדים רבים נמנעים מדג עם חלב, אך היקף המנהג שונה.

halacha_index.summary: Sephardim name children after living grandparents as an act of kibbud av va'em.
common_practices: Naming after the newborn's living grandparents is considered an honor
halacha_index.source: shulchanaruchharav.com, 'Naming one's son or daughter after one's father or mother while they're still alive' (citing Yalkut Me'am Lo'ez Shemot 20:12); Chabad.org, 'The Laws of Jewish Names'
halacha_index.review_notes: The source clarifies this refers to naming after the newborn's grandparents, not after a living parent himself. A claimed order (husband's parents before wife's) appears only in a popular source and is excluded pending review.

references.title: ⚖️ Daily Halacha: Naming one’s son or daughter after one’s father or mother (the Grandparent of the newborn) while they’re still alive

halacha_index.topic_he: קריאת שם על שם סבים חיים
halacha_index.summary_he: ספרדים קוראים לילדים על שם סבים חיים כמעשה כיבוד אב ואם.

halacha_index.summary: In the Western rite, the memorial prayer is the Hashkabah (hashcaba), and the anniversary of death is called the nahala.

variants.practice: A hashcaba is chanted at the conclusion of services; men may receive an aliyah on the Shabbat morning following a loved one's nahala, at which time a hashcaba is recited; Shearith Israel states the Nahala is also observed on the 30th day from the date of burial and in the 11th month from the date of burial. Separate male and female hashcaba forms exist in the melody repertoire.
variants.source: Congregation Shearith Israel, 'Life Cycle Events'; sandpcentral.org, 'Melodies (alphabetical)'

halacha_index.source: Congregation Shearith Israel, Life Cycle Events
halacha_index.review_notes: Eastern Sephardi hashkava and yahrzeit (azkara/nahala) customs were not documented from a primary source in this pass.
halacha_index.summary_he: בנוסח המערבי תפילת הזיכרון היא ההשכבה (hashcaba), ויום השנה לפטירה נקרא נחלה.

halacha_index.summary: Aleppo (Syrian) and Moroccan communities rise in the small hours of winter Shabbat mornings to sing bakashot until the morning service.
common_practices: Sung in winter, beginning on Shabbat Bereshit

variants.practice: Fixed order sung each week, from the Miqra Qodesh collection compiled by R. Mordechai Abadi (Aleppo, 1872); season runs until Shabbat HaGadol; Ades Synagogue, Jerusalem is a center.
variants.source: Jewish Music Research Centre, Hebrew University, 'Baqqashah (Pl. Baqqashot)'; The New Arab (Hadar Cohen)

variants.practice: Different bakashot each week from Shir Yedidot (Marrakesh 1921), organized by Andalusian musical modes; season runs until Shabbat Zakhor; revived in Israel by R. David Buzaglo.
variants.source: Jewish Music Research Centre, Hebrew University, 'Baqqashah (Pl. Baqqashot)'

halacha_index.source: Jewish Music Research Centre, Hebrew University of Jerusalem, 'Baqqashah (Pl. Baqqashot)'
halacha_index.review_notes: Many piyyutim are by R. Israel Najara (Zemirot Yisrael). Amsterdam reportedly retains a few bakashot before the Shabbat service (unverified lead).
halacha_index.summary_he: קהילות חלב (סוריה) ומרוקו קמות בשעות הקטנות של בוקר שבתות החורף לשיר בקשות עד תפילת הבוקר.

unique_minhagim.name: Mimouna
unique_minhagim.description: Moroccan/Maghrebi open-house celebration with sweets and blessings at the end of Pesach.
unique_minhagim.when: Night and day after the last day of Pesach
unique_minhagim.source: My Jewish Learning, 'Mimouna: A Post-Passover Celebration'
unique_minhagim.description_he: חגיגת בית פתוח מרוקאית/מגרבית עם ממתקים וברכות בסוף פסח.

unique_minhagim.name: Bakashot (Shirat HaBakashot)
unique_minhagim.description: Pre-dawn singing of kabbalistic piyyutim on winter Shabbatot; fixed weekly order in Aleppo tradition, rotating weekly in Moroccan tradition.
unique_minhagim.when: Shabbat Bereshit to Shabbat Zakhor (Moroccan) or Shabbat HaGadol (Aleppo)
unique_minhagim.source: Jewish Music Research Centre, Hebrew University, 'Baqqashah (Pl. Baqqashot)'
unique_minhagim.description_he: שירת פיוטים קבליים לפני עלות השחר בשבתות החורף; סדר שבועי קבוע במסורת חלב, וסדר מתחלף מדי שבוע במסורת המרוקאית.

unique_minhagim.name: Rosh Hashana seder of simanim
unique_minhagim.description: Structured sequence of symbolic foods with Yehi Ratzon formulas, ordered per Ben Ish Chai beginning with dates.
unique_minhagim.source: Shulchan Arukh OC 583:1; Ben Ish Chai, Nitzavim 4
unique_minhagim.description_he: רצף מובנה של מאכלי סמל עם נוסחי "יהי רצון", מסודר לפי הבן איש חי ומתחיל בתמרים.

unique_minhagim.name: Hashkabah
unique_minhagim.description: Spanish-Portuguese memorial prayer chanted at the end of services and on the Shabbat after a nahala.
unique_minhagim.when: After services; Shabbat after the nahala; Rosh Hodesh and Yom Kippur for the perpetual list
unique_minhagim.source: Congregation Shearith Israel, Life Cycle Events
unique_minhagim.description_he: תפילת זיכרון ספרדית-פורטוגזית הנאמרת בסוף התפילות ובשבת אחרי נחלה.

unique_minhagim.name: Morir habemos greeting
unique_minhagim.description: Judeo-Spanish exchange on Tisha B'Av ('Morir habemos' / 'Ya lo sabemos') in Amsterdam and New York S&P congregations.
unique_minhagim.source: London Sephardi Minhag, 'Fast of Ab' page
unique_minhagim.description_he: החלפת דברים ביהודית-ספרדית בתשעה באב ("Morir habemos" / "Ya lo sabemos") בקהילות ספרדיות-פורטוגזיות באמסטרדם ובניו יורק.

Candle-lighting blessing order: most Sephardim bless before lighting (Yechaveh Da'at 2:33); some families keep blessing after

Omer end: morning of the 34th (Shulchan Arukh, most Israeli Sephardim) vs Lag BaOmer (Turkish and Egyptian communities) vs erev Shavuot for haircuts (Ari's followers)
